Thousands in Spain's capital protest increasing housing costs
Stream on stream logo
Thousands have rallied in central Madrid against spiraling housing costs that have priced many Spaniards out of the market
By ALICIA LEON Associated Press
May 24, 2026, 6:52 AM
1:49
Stream on stream logo
People take part during a protest in Madrid, Spain, on Sunday, May 24, 2026, against rising housing costs that are pricing many Spaniards out of the market amid a broader housing crisis in Spain. (AP Photo/Manu Fernandez)
The Associated Press
Stream on stream logo
MADRID -- Thousands of people rallied in central Madrid on Sunday against spiraling housing costs that have priced many Spaniards out of the housing market despite a recent economic boom, particularly in cities such as the country's capital and Barcelona.
Stream on stream logo
The country has a strong tradition of homeownership and scant public housing for rent, while rents have been driven up by increased demand, including due to tourism and population growth linked to immigration, analysts say.
The protesters chanted slogans and held banners highlighting their right to housing.
Stream on stream logo
Last month, Spain’ s government passed a sweeping plan worth 7 billion euros ($8.23 billion) to build more public housing over the next four years and provide help for young renters and homebuyers, among the hardest hit by high rental and home costs.

citations.title: Could Maricarmen’s eviction force Spain’s high rental costs to change? - CSMonitor.com
excerpts:
Instagram
Madrid | Oct. 02, 2026, 4:33 p.m. ET | 5 min read
Evictions are a daily occurrence across Spain, rarely drawing much public attention. Until last week, that is.
The entire population watched in shock as an elderly woman was pulled out of the Madrid apartment – where she had lived since 1956 – on a stretcher.
Police beat protesters attempting to stop the eviction of María del Carmen Abascal, now known countrywide as Maricarmen.
What began as one woman’s story quickly morphed into something much bigger. Protesters took to the streets in Madrid and beyond, their anger fueled not just by Ms.
Abascal’s treatment, but by the skyrocketing housing prices that many cannot afford themselves.
Why we wrote this
Maricarmen’s eviction may have sparked current protests, but Spain has been rife with frustration over high housing costs for years. Is there sufficient political will to get something done now?
Abascal.
The burden of rent
The left-leaning government has proposed a series of fixes in response to the protests, including prohibiting evictions of vulnerable residents until 2030, preventing “vulture funds” from buying property until 2028, and extending current rental agreements for two extra years.
A separate decree would make rental agreements indefinite, forcing landlords to compensate renters if they break a contract. Both sets of proposals were voted down Friday in Congress.
Protesters deemed the reforms insufficient regardless. A basic tenet of the movement is that housing should be a right, not a business.
Yet others say neither supply-side measures that regulate landlords nor demand-side approaches that protect renters have made a lasting difference on costs in cities like London and Paris.

Spain faces housing protests in more than 50 cities after parliament rejects tenant protections
Protest are expected in Madrid and other major cities
Protest are expected in Madrid and other major cities - Copyright AP Photo
Copyright AP Photo
By Simon Ormiston
Published on 03/10/2026 - 9:34 GMT+2
Share Comments Add Euronews on Google
Share Close Button
The eviction of an 87-year-old woman has turned anger over rents that have nearly doubled in ten years into a threat to Pedro Sánchez's minority government.
Demonstrators are set to march in more than 50 Spanish cities on Saturday, a day after parliament voted down two government decrees meant to give tenants stronger protection.
ADVERTISEMENT
ADVERTISEMENT
The Tenants' Union, which has been coordinating the protests, called the demonstrations.
Activists have already been camped for about a week in Puerta del Sol, one of the capital's main tourist squares.
The anger was triggered by the eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal, who was carried out on a stretcher from the Madrid flat where she had lived for around seven decades.
Housing campaigners say an investment company had bought the property and sought to raise her rent by 275 percent. After the backlash, the new owners agreed to let her return at a low rent.
Average rents have almost doubled over the past decade and asking prices for homes are up about 90 percent, according to the real estate website Idealista.
